title: Rickettsial Clues: RMSF Rash, Eschars, Brill-Zinsser and the Weil-Felix Test
summary: Recognise the inward-marching RMSF rash, the infections that leave an inoculation eschar, Brill-Zinsser disease as relapsing epidemic typhus, and why the Weil-Felix test should give way to IFA or PCR.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 63 Hit 3 (RMSF rash), Hit 7 (Brill-Zinsser disease), Hit 8 (eschar-associated infections), Hit 9 (Weil-Felix) and Trap 2 (Weil-Felix). Checked against Biggs 2016 (CDC MMWR RR-65(2)), Stewart 2021, Koh 2010, De Vito 2020, Consigny 2005, Krusell 2002, Faucher 2012, Bechah 2010 and Gillespie 2009. Biggs gives rash onset as 2–4 days after fever onset (the reviewer says days 3–5) and gives no percentage for RMSF palm/sole involvement; the reviewer’s “50%” is not taught (register flag rv-rmsf-palms-soles-50). Weil-Felix is taught as unreliable rather than unavailable, because open reviews note it remains the only test in some resource-limited settings (register flag rv-weil-felix-resource-limited). Not taught: select-agent status, cat scratch disease, Q fever transmission.

objectives: Describe the onset, spread and timing of the Rocky Mountain spotted fever rash.
Name rickettsial infections that typically produce an inoculation eschar and contrast them with RMSF.
Explain Brill-Zinsser disease as recrudescent epidemic typhus.
Explain why the Weil-Felix test is unreliable and which tests replace it.

scenes.title: Three fevers, three skin clues
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three febrile patients. (1) A hiker in the eastern United States, fever for 3 days, now small pink spots on the wrists and ankles, no scab anywhere. (2) A traveller back from a safari in South Africa with fever and several black scabs on the legs. (3) A 74-year-old who survived epidemic typhus as a young man, now febrile with no lice and no travel. A clinic asks the lab for a Weil-Felix test on all three. Question token: “Which clue points where, and which test?”

cues.text: Three fevers arrive. A hiker with pink spots starting on the wrists and ankles, and no scab. A safari traveller with several black scabs on the legs.
And an older man who had epidemic typhus decades ago, now febrile, with no lice and no travel.
The clinic asks for a Weil-Felix test on all three. Which clue points where, and is that the right test?

props.label: Which clue points where, and which test?

scenes.title: The RMSF rash marches inward
scenes.altText: Schematic body outline with arrows from wrists and ankles toward the trunk. Cards (CDC 2016 guidance): Rocky Mountain spotted fever (Rickettsia rickettsii) rash typically appears 2–4 days after fever onset; it begins as small (1–5 mm) blanching pink macules on the ankles, wrists or forearms, then spreads to the palms, soles, arms, legs and trunk, usually sparing the face; it becomes maculopapular, sometimes with central petechiae. A generalised petechial rash including palms and soles usually appears by day 5 or 6 and indicates advanced disease. Fewer than half of patients have a rash in the first 3 days, and some never develop one. An inoculation eschar is rarely present in RMSF.

cues.text: Rocky Mountain spotted fever, caused by Rickettsia rickettsii, has a rash that typically appears two to four days after the fever starts.
It begins as small, blanching pink spots on the ankles, wrists or forearms, then spreads to the palms, soles, limbs and trunk, usually sparing the face.
A petechial rash on the palms and soles usually appears by day five or six, and it signals advanced disease, so it is a late finding, not an early one.
Fewer than half of patients have a rash in the first three days, some never get one, and an eschar is rare in this disease. No rash does not mean no RMSF.

scenes.title: Eschar: the door the organism used
scenes.altText: Schematic eschar: a dark, scabbed plaque over a shallow ulcer with a red, indurated halo at the bite site (the CDC guidance describes the Rickettsia parkeri eschar as typically 0.5–2 cm). Map of eschar-associated infections: scrub typhus (Orientia tsutsugamushi, trombiculid mites; eschar supports the diagnosis but is variably present); Mediterranean spotted fever (Rickettsia conorii; eschar usually single, the “tache noir”, seen in about 58–64% of patients in one review); African tick-bite fever (Rickettsia africae; one or more eschars, multiple eschars in 7 of 10 French travellers in one outbreak report); rickettsialpox (Rickettsia akari, mite-borne; classic eschar with a vesicular rash); Rickettsia parkeri in the Americas (eschar as first sign in nearly all patients). Contrast: eschar in under 1% of RMSF in one review.

cues.text: An eschar is a dark, scabbed plaque over a shallow ulcer, with a red halo, at the place where the tick or mite fed. It marks the inoculation site.

Think scrub typhus, caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi and spread by trombiculid mites; an eschar supports the diagnosis, but it is not always present. Mediterranean spotted fever, from Rickettsia conorii, usually has a single eschar, the tache noir.

African tick-bite fever, from Rickettsia africae, can leave one or several eschars; in one outbreak among French travellers, seven of ten had multiple eschars. Rickettsialpox, from mite-borne Rickettsia akari, pairs an eschar with a vesicular rash.
In the Americas, Rickettsia parkeri starts with an eschar in nearly all patients. Rocky Mountain spotted fever is the contrast: an eschar is rare.

props.label: R. parkeri: eschar in nearly all

scenes.title: Weil-Felix, better tests, and a ghost of typhus
scenes.altText: Weil-Felix card: a heterophile agglutination test using Proteus antigens (OX-19, OX-2, OX-K) that cross-react with rickettsial antibodies; in one review’s table, sensitivity 21–70% and specificity 46–96% for spotted fever group rickettsioses; now rarely used, though in some resource-limited settings it is the only test available. Better card: IgG IFA on paired sera is the reference serology; PCR is far more sensitive on tissue than blood, up to 92% on eschar samples; eschar biopsy or swab is a useful specimen. Brill-Zinsser card: latent Rickettsia prowazekii can persist for years or decades after epidemic typhus and recrudesce as a milder illness unrelated to new louse infestation; recrudescent patients can act as a source for lice. Hook answers.

cues.text: The Weil-Felix test is a heterophile agglutination: Proteus antigens such as OX-19, OX-2 and OX-K cross-react with antibodies against rickettsiae. Its sensitivity and specificity are both poor.
IgG immunofluorescence on paired sera is the reference serology. For direct detection, PCR works far better on tissue than on blood, especially on an eschar biopsy or swab.

Brill-Zinsser disease is a relapse of epidemic typhus. Rickettsia prowazekii stays latent for years or decades, then recrudesces as a milder illness, without any new lice. If lice are present, the patient can pass the organism on.
Back to the hook: the hiker fits early RMSF, the safari traveller fits African tick-bite fever, and the typhus survivor fits Brill-Zinsser disease. For all three, ask for IFA or PCR, not Weil-Felix.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A positive Weil-Felix confirms a rickettsiosis” (✓ poor sensitivity and specificity; confirm with IFA or PCR); “No eschar, so not rickettsial” (✓ eschar is rare in RMSF and variable in scrub typhus); “Brill-Zinsser needs a new louse bite” (✓ it is recrudescence of latent Rickettsia prowazekii years later).

cues.text: Trap one: a positive Weil-Felix confirms a rickettsiosis. No: it is insensitive and nonspecific. Confirm with immunofluorescence or PCR.
Trap two: no eschar, so it is not rickettsial. No: an eschar is rare in Rocky Mountain spotted fever and variable in scrub typhus.
Trap three: Brill-Zinsser disease needs a new louse bite. No: it is latent Rickettsia prowazekii waking up years later.

scenes.altText: Memory aid: “RMSF paints from the EDGES IN; an eschar is the DOOR MARK where the organism entered; Brill-Zinsser is an OLD TENANT waking up in the house; Weil-Felix asks a STRANGER (Proteus) to identify the culprit.” Tokens: edges in = RMSF rash · door mark = eschar · old tenant = Brill-Zinsser · stranger = Weil-Felix. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: RMSF paints from the edges in. An eschar is the door mark where the organism entered. Brill-Zinsser is an old tenant waking up. And Weil-Felix asks a stranger, Proteus, to identify the culprit.

Where it breaks: the RMSF rash can be late, atypical or absent; eschar frequency varies by species and many patients with scrub typhus have none; and in some resource-limited settings, Weil-Felix is still the only test available.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “RMSF rash: wrists and ankles inward · palms and soles late · eschar rare”, “Eschar → scrub typhus, conorii, africae, akari · Brill-Zinsser = latent typhus · IFA or PCR, not Weil-Felix”.

cues.text: The Rocky Mountain spotted fever rash starts at the wrists and ankles and rarely comes with an eschar, an eschar points to scrub typhus or an eschar-forming spotted fever group infection, Brill-Zinsser disease is latent epidemic typhus returning, and Weil-Felix is too weak to replace immunofluorescence or PCR.

props.label: RMSF: wrists/ankles inward · palms, soles late · eschar rare
Eschar → Orientia, conorii, africae, akari · Brill = relapse · IFA/PCR

explanation.what: Plain language: the skin gives clues. Rocky Mountain spotted fever spots start on the wrists and ankles and spread inward; a black scab at a bite site points to other rickettsial infections; an old typhus infection can wake up decades later; and an old, cheap agglutination test with Proteus bacteria is not reliable enough to confirm any of these. Scientific terms: Rickettsia rickettsii, maculopapular and petechial rash, inoculation eschar (tache noir), Orientia tsutsugamushi, Rickettsia conorii, Rickettsia africae, Rickettsia akari, Rickettsia parkeri, Rickettsia prowazekii, recrudescence, heterophile agglutination, Proteus OX-19/OX-2/OX-K, indirect immunofluorescence assay (IFA), PCR.
explanation.why: Rickettsiae infect endothelial cells, producing vascular rash; the organism is inoculated at the feeding site, where some species cause a local eschar in which organisms are more concentrated than in rash lesions. Rickettsia prowazekii can persist in a recovered host and reactivate. Proteus OX antigens share cross-reacting epitopes with rickettsiae, so the Weil-Felix reaction is indirect and imprecise.
explanation.measure: RMSF rash: 2–4 days after fever onset; ankles, wrists, forearms → palms, soles, limbs, trunk; palms and soles petechial by day 5–6 (advanced disease); < 50% with rash in first 3 days. Eschar: under 1% of RMSF; variable in scrub typhus; usually single in R. conorii; often several in R. africae. Weil-Felix (spotted fever group): sensitivity 21–70%, specificity 46–96%. PCR on eschar up to 92% sensitive.
explanation.differs: RMSF (rash from extremities inward, eschar rare) vs eschar-associated rickettsioses (scab at bite site); Brill-Zinsser (latent relapse, milder, no new lice) vs primary epidemic typhus (louse-borne); Weil-Felix (heterophile, Proteus) vs IFA (specific rickettsial antigens) vs PCR (DNA, best on tissue).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: name the infection from a rash pattern or eschar, recognise Brill-Zinsser in an older patient with past typhus and no lice, or choose IFA or PCR over Weil-Felix.

questions.stem: A patient in the United States has had fever for 3 days after a tick bite. Small blanching pink macules appeared on the wrists and ankles and are spreading toward the trunk. No eschar is found. Which infection best fits?

options.rationale: Correct. The RMSF rash classically begins on the ankles, wrists or forearms and spreads inward, and an eschar is rarely present.
Incorrect. Scrub typhus is spread by trombiculid mites in East and Southeast Asia and northern Australia, and an eschar supports that diagnosis.
Incorrect. Rickettsialpox is mite-borne and typically shows an eschar with a vesicular rash.
Incorrect. This is recrudescent epidemic typhus in a person with past infection, not an acute tick-borne illness.

questions.stem: A traveller returns from South Africa with fever, headache and several black, scabbed lesions with red halos on the legs. Which organism is most likely?

options.rationale: Correct. African tick-bite fever produces one or more inoculation eschars; multiple eschars are a key clue.
Incorrect. RMSF occurs in the Americas, and an eschar is rare in it.
Incorrect. Epidemic typhus is louse-borne, and an eschar is not a feature of it.
Incorrect. Murine typhus is flea-borne, and an eschar is not a feature of it.

questions.stem: A clinician requests a Weil-Felix test to diagnose a suspected rickettsial infection. Which response is best?

options.text: Recommend IgG IFA on paired sera, and PCR on an eschar or skin biopsy where available
options.rationale: Correct. IFA is the reference serology; PCR is far more sensitive on tissue such as an eschar than on blood.

options.text: Run Weil-Felix; a positive result confirms the diagnosis
options.rationale: Incorrect. Weil-Felix uses cross-reacting Proteus antigens and has poor sensitivity and specificity.

options.text: Run Weil-Felix; a negative result rules out a rickettsiosis
options.rationale: Incorrect. Its sensitivity is low (21–70% for spotted fever group in one review), so a negative does not exclude disease.

options.text: Culture the blood on routine agar
options.rationale: Incorrect. Rickettsiae are obligate intracellular bacteria and do not grow on routine media.

claims.text: RMSF rash timing, start at ankles/wrists/forearms, inward spread sparing the face, palms/soles late (day 5–6, advanced disease); rash may be absent early or never; eschar rare.
Reviewer: palms/soles involved in 50% of RMSF.
claims.note: Not taught. Biggs 2016 gives no percentage for RMSF palm/sole involvement (it gives about half for R. parkeri).

claims.text: Eschar description; eschar-associated infections: scrub typhus (variable), R. conorii (usually single), R. africae (one or more, often multiple), R. akari (eschar plus vesicular rash), R. parkeri (nearly all).

Rickettsiae infect vascular endothelial cells and are obligate intracellular bacteria that do not grow on routine media; eschars hold more organisms than rash lesions; Weil-Felix relies on cross-reacting Proteus antigens.
Brill-Zinsser disease: latent R. prowazekii recrudescing years to decades later, milder, unrelated to new louse infestation; patients can be a source for lice.
Weil-Felix: Proteus OX heterophile agglutination with poor sensitivity and specificity; IFA reference serology; PCR better on eschar/tissue than blood.
Scenario invented; body, rash and eschar drawings schematic.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 63 Hit 9 and Trap 2 call the Weil-Felix test obsolete and say not to use it. Stewart 2021 and De Vito 2020 agree it has poor sensitivity and specificity and is no longer first-line, but note it remains the only test available in some resource-limited settings; the lesson teaches it as unreliable and to be replaced by IFA or PCR where available (register flag rv-weil-felix-resource-limited).

Ch. 63 Hit 3 states palms/soles are involved in 50% of RMSF. Biggs 2016 describes palm/sole involvement as appearing by day 5–6 and indicating advanced disease but gives no percentage; the figure is not taught (register flag rv-rmsf-palms-soles-50).
